chunks: LiPo discharge and charge curves. The question: Explain the LiPo discharge and charge curve.
Discharge and charge curves are graphs of a cell's voltage as it empties or fills. On discharge, the voltage starts near 4.
2 volts, drifts down slowly through a long flat stretch, then falls off a cliff near empty. On charge, a charger first pushes a constant current until the voltage reaches 4.
2 volts, then holds 4. 2 volts while the current tapers away.
Picture a ski run. It begins with a short steep drop, then a long, gentle slope that takes up most of the run, and then a sharp drop right at the end. That is the discharge curve.
The long gentle slope is why voltage is a poor sign of how full the battery is: skiers on it all look about the same height.
And the final cliff comes fast, so the device has to stop in time.
The backbone. The steep foot below 10 % and the climb above 90 % are where the discharge cliff and the charge CV phase happen; the shallow middle is the plateau.
Plateau: the long, nearly flat middle of the discharge curve, from about 3. 9 volts to 3. 6 volts. Knee: the point near the end where the voltage starts to drop faster.
Cutoff voltage: where discharge stops, about 3. 0 volts ("LiPo cell voltage range and why").
CC/CV charging: constant current, then constant voltage ("Constant-current and constant-voltage charge phases").
Internal resistance: it shifts the whole curve down by current times resistance ("Battery internal resistance").
Take a 2 Ah cell with 50 milliohms of resistance, discharged at 1C, which is 2 amps. The moment the load connects, the voltage steps down by 2 times 0. 05 equals 0. 1 volts.
Then it follows the plateau and ends at the cutoff. Charging the same cell at 1C, the voltage climbs to 4. 2 volts in about 51 minutes, when the cell is about 85% full. Holding 4.
2 volts then takes about another 26 minutes for the last part. That is the whole idea.
"Discharge: a full cell is 4. 2 volts, drops by I times R when loaded, then follows a long plateau around 3. 6 to 3. 8 volts, with a knee near 3. 4 and a cliff at the 3.
0 volts cutoff. More current or cold slides it down and ends it sooner. Charge is constant current until the cell hits 4.
2 volts, with the voltage rising, then constant voltage at 4. 2 volts while the current decays exponentially, terminating at about C over 20.
In a model, 1C gets to about 85 percent in 51 minutes, and the CV tail takes another 26."
